title: Fed's Waller Backs December Rate Hike and Opens Door to Half-Point Move
excerpt: Governor Christopher Waller said he would back at least a quarter-point increase on December 8-9 even if inflation cooled — and October core CPI then rose exactly the 0.3% he had named as the bar for considering 50 basis points.
body:
• Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday he would support at least a 25-basis-point rate hike at the December 8-9 FOMC meeting, even if October inflation improved.
  • Waller set a clear bar for a bigger move: if core CPI rose 0.3% or more in October, a 50-basis-point hike should be considered. Hours later, official data showed core CPI rose exactly 0.3%, for the third month in a row.
  • Before the data, futures priced about an 85% chance of a December hike to a 4.00%-4.25% target range; after the data, market odds of a half-point move rose to about 15%.
  • For US borrowers: a December hike would lift the policy rate to 4.00%-4.25%, keeping upward pressure on mortgage rates, car loans and credit-card APRs into the new year.

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller has backed another increase in US interest rates next month, and set out the exact condition under which he would consider going bigger. Speaking in London on Tuesday, hours before the October inflation report, Waller said he would support a quarter-point hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December 8-9 meeting even if the data showed price pressures cooling.

"While I am hoping for an improvement over September, even if this occurs, I would still support a 25 basis point increase in the FOMC's policy rate at our December meeting," Waller said in remarks prepared for delivery at a conference hosted by King's Business School and the Money Macro & Finance Society, according to Reuters. If core consumer prices rose 0.3% or more from September, he added, "a stronger policy move may be needed" and "a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting."

"We need to raise rates to put downward pressure on inflation."

— Christopher Waller, Federal Reserve Governor

Waller, whom President Donald Trump appointed to the Fed's Board of Governors in 2020, also said policy "has been not nearly as restrictive as I thought" and that real rates have to rise to maintain the current level of restrictiveness, according to Reuters reporting carried by FXStreet. His comments contrast with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who has resisted giving any rate-path guidance at all.

Then the inflation data met his bar

The October Consumer Price Index, released later on Tuesday, landed precisely on Waller's trigger. Headline CPI rose 0.4% month over month, down from September's 0.6% as energy inflation receded but above the 0.3% economists polled by Reuters had forecast. Core CPI, which strips out food and energy, rose 0.3% for the third consecutive month — the reading Waller had said would prompt him to consider a half-point hike.

Markets moved quickly. Reuters reported that a quarter-point December hike is now all but assured, bets on a larger increase were building through the morning to close to 15%, and bonds sold off broadly. Rate futures as of Monday's close had priced about an 85% chance of a December hike to a new target range of 4.00%-4.25%, and a better-than-even chance of another hike as soon as March.

Where policy stands

The Fed raised its benchmark rate in September, its first increase since July 2023, and then held in October, leaving the target range at 3.75% to 4.00%. Waller said he backed the October pause partly because policymakers had all but promised further tightening — and warned that failing to deliver hikes the Fed has communicated would put its credibility at risk.

He is not the only official leaning hawkish. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said on Tuesday the central bank needs at least two more quarter-point increases, delivered possibly promptly, to stop broadening price pressures from becoming embedded. A Reuters poll of 101 economists conducted November 6-10 found a majority expect the Fed to hike once more in December to 4.00%-4.25% and then stop, with 55% of forecasters expecting December to mark the end of the current cycle. That consensus now faces a live question Waller put on the table: not whether December brings a hike, but whether it brings 25 or 50 basis points.

What it means for borrowers

Rate hikes raise the cost of borrowing across the economy. A move to 4.00%-4.25% — and especially a half-point step — would keep pressure on mortgage rates, auto loans and credit-card APRs at a time when household budgets are already stretched, and would support the dollar against other currencies. The FOMC decides on December 8-9; between now and then, every inflation and jobs print will be read against the bar Waller set in London.
